title: USPA Tandem Instructor Evaluation Practice
description: Original practice flashcards based on the uploaded 2026 IRM tandem evaluation requirements, scoring rubrics, tandem techniques and teaching guidance. These are not official exam questions or a promise of what an examiner will ask.
sourcePolicy: Cites the uploaded IRM revision. Manufacturer procedures and the examiner’s briefed jump plan must also be followed. Planned dive-flow altitudes are distinguished from automatic-failure thresholds.

usage.scoringRule: For included cards, compare selected option id to correctOptionId.
usage.recallMode: Hide choices, recall the answer, then reveal answer/explanation.
usage.practiceMode: Use non-null practicePrompt to rehearse a teaching or supervision skill. Flashcard scores are not a practical rating sign-off.
usage.compatibility: Uses the original Sigma deck’s core cards/options/correctOptionId/answer/explanation/references/includeInQuiz fields. These generated choices contain no letter-dependent answers.
usage.sourceLinks: pdfPage is 1-based; printedPage is the IRM footer page, not the embedded SIM page.

cards.question: Which three areas does the IRM evaluate?

options.text: Written answers, packing speed, and jump count.
Freefall, tracking, and reserve packing only.
Aircraft handling, rigging, and canopy design.
Ground training, supervision, and air skills.

cards.answer: Ground training, supervision, and air skills.
cards.explanation: You must demonstrate observation, evaluation and correction of the simulated student across the three areas.

cards.question: What is the minimum passing evaluation score?

options.text: 100%, regardless of automatic failures.
At least 75%, even with one automatic failure.
At least 75%, with no automatic unsatisfactory result.
At least 50%, if the landing is safe.

cards.answer: At least 75%, with no automatic unsatisfactory result.
cards.explanation: An automatic unsatisfactory result overrides the numerical score; this is distinct from the Sigma written examination requirement.

cards.question: Which two ground lessons must a USPA TI candidate pass?

options.text: Category A and Category B.
Category C and Category D.
Two Category G lessons.
Category A and Category H.

cards.answer: Category A and Category B.
cards.explanation: The tandem-instructor row lists Category A and B ground evaluations.
cards.practicePrompt: Teach each lesson to a simulated student using a complete lesson plan.

cards.question: Which two air evaluations must a USPA TI candidate pass?

options.text: Two solo Sigma jumps.
One demonstration tandem and one HandCam tandem.
A Category A tandem dive plan and a Category B tandem dive plan.
Two Category G formation jumps.

cards.answer: A Category A tandem dive plan and a Category B tandem dive plan.
cards.explanation: Both are supervised by a USPA Tandem Instructor Examiner.

cards.question: How many attempts are available to pass the two ground evaluations?

options.text: Four total attempts.
Unlimited attempts during the course.
Two attempts for each of four lessons.
Fifteen total attempts.

cards.answer: Four total attempts.
cards.explanation: Failure to pass the required two within four attempts fails the ground-evaluation portion; the IRM has separate retesting provisions.

cards.question: How many attempts are available to pass the two TI air evaluations?

options.text: Ten total attempts.
Unlimited attempts.
Four total attempts.
Fifteen total attempts.

cards.answer: Four total attempts.
cards.explanation: Do not confuse this USPA limit with the manufacturer course’s attempt allowance.

cards.question: Who can act as the simulated student on the USPA TI air-evaluation jumps?

options.text: Any jumper with an A license.
Any jumper with 50 jumps, regardless of rating.
Any first-time passenger who signs a waiver.
A jumper who holds or has held a USPA Coach or higher rating and receives the examiner briefing.

cards.answer: A jumper who holds or has held a USPA Coach or higher rating and receives the examiner briefing.
cards.explanation: The tandem examiner supervises and briefs the front rider on procedures.

cards.question: When does the supervision evaluation begin and end?

options.text: It begins at the door and ends at opening.
It begins with collecting jump equipment and ends after completing the debrief.
It starts on boarding and ends at exit.
It begins at opening and ends at touchdown.

cards.answer: It begins with collecting jump equipment and ends after completing the debrief.
cards.explanation: Supervision pauses during the air-evaluation phase, then resumes through canopy flight, return and debrief.

cards.question: When does the air-evaluation phase begin and end?

options.text: From deployment until the debrief.
From exit until returning to the packing area.
From directing door/step setup until the group’s parachutes are open.
From manifesting until boarding.

cards.answer: From directing door/step setup until the group’s parachutes are open.
cards.explanation: The IRM specifies the phase boundaries; supervision resumes after opening.

cards.question: When may the candidate call a time-out during an evaluation?

options.text: At any time to restart the lesson.
For safety reasons.
Whenever the score seems low.
Whenever a teaching point is forgotten.

cards.answer: For safety reasons.
cards.explanation: The evaluator may call a time-out when necessary. The candidate’s exception is safety.

cards.question: Whose altimeter is the reference for scoring when readings differ slightly?

options.text: The average of everyone’s readings.
The evaluator’s altimeter.
The candidate’s audible.
The student’s wrist altimeter.

cards.answer: The evaluator’s altimeter.
cards.explanation: The IRM identifies the evaluator’s altimeter as the scoring reference.

cards.question: What is the general IRM minimum exit altitude for TI evaluation jumps?

options.text: 7,500 ft MSL in every course jump.
9,500 ft MSL, regardless of terrain.
9,500 ft AGL; additionally meet the applicable manufacturer jump requirements.
4,000 ft AGL.

cards.answer: 9,500 ft AGL; additionally meet the applicable manufacturer jump requirements.
cards.explanation: The IRM’s IAD/static-line Category B exception is not a tandem exception. UPT can require higher exits for particular course jumps.

cards.question: What teaching structure is explicitly required to avoid a ground-evaluation auto unsat?

options.text: Explain every detail before any demonstration.
Whole-part-whole.
Lecture-test-jump only.
Have the student watch repeatedly without practice.

cards.answer: Whole-part-whole.
cards.explanation: Failure to use whole-part-whole is one of five listed ground automatic failures.
cards.practicePrompt: Demonstrate the whole task, practice and correct its parts, then reassemble it.

cards.question: How should the first whole demonstration be presented?

options.text: Only verbal instructions without a demo or overview.
A lengthy narration of every movement repeated several times.
An intentionally incorrect performance for the student to imitate.
An accurate big-picture demonstration with minimal detail.

cards.answer: An accurate big-picture demonstration with minimal detail.
cards.explanation: Use an accurate physical demonstration or video; develop details while the student actively participates.

cards.question: What should guide a lesson’s goals?

options.text: Only what makes a good video.
The number of minutes available alone.
The instructor’s favorite exercises regardless of progression.
The student’s starting point and measurable ISP advancement goals.

cards.answer: The student’s starting point and measurable ISP advancement goals.
cards.explanation: Assess the student using their logbook, progression card and relevant questions; state clear goals with measurable outcomes.

cards.question: What two questions help select the teaching strategy for each skill?

options.text: Is it review or new, and is it mostly doing or thinking?
Is the student visual or auditory, and is the instructor tired?
Can I skip it, and can someone else sign it off?
Is it easy or hard, and is the student tall or short?

cards.answer: Is it review or new, and is it mostly doing or thinking?
cards.explanation: The IRM uses familiarity and skill type to select active teaching strategies.

cards.question: How should you teach a familiar physical skill?

options.text: Ask the student to show you, observe, and correct imperfections.
Repeat the full lecture before letting them move.
Assume it is mastered because it was signed off.
Change any correct technique to your own preference.

cards.answer: Ask the student to show you, observe, and correct imperfections.
cards.explanation: This is Review-Do: observe actual performance and retain previously learned techniques that are correct.

cards.question: How should you introduce a new physical skill?

options.text: Demonstrate slowly, have the student copy, correct, and progress to independent real-time performance.
Require a full-speed attempt with no demonstration.
Explain it once and move on.
Let the student watch without performing it.

cards.answer: Demonstrate slowly, have the student copy, correct, and progress to independent real-time performance.
cards.explanation: This is New-Do; the student performs while you supply feedback.

cards.question: What should you do when a student practices a movement incorrectly?

options.text: Wait until the jump to mention it.
Only tell them the whole attempt was bad.
Let several incorrect repetitions build confidence.
Stop and correct the error promptly with positive, specific guidance.

cards.answer: Stop and correct the error promptly with positive, specific guidance.
cards.explanation: Failure to observe and correct is a ground auto unsat; prompt correction prevents an incorrect habit.
cards.practicePrompt: Have a simulated student misplace a foot in exit practice and give a specific correction.

cards.question: Which set lists all five ground-evaluation automatic failures?

options.text: No HandCam; no outside video; no stand-up landing; slow packing; no coach license.
Late manifesting; bad spot; poor landing; wrong target; missed debrief.
Low exam score; long classroom session; small mockup; no projector; no whiteboard.
No whole-part-whole; missing/incorrect information; insufficient repetition; insufficient specific direction; failure to observe/correct.

cards.answer: No whole-part-whole; missing/incorrect information; insufficient repetition; insufficient specific direction; failure to observe/correct.
cards.explanation: These are the ground auto-unsat list, distinct from the tandem supervision and air lists.
cards.practicePrompt: Recite all five and explain how your lesson prevents each.

cards.question: What is the purpose of variable practice?

options.text: Let errors continue without correction.
Prepare the student to solve problems when events differ from the ideal plan.
Create confusion with unrelated tasks.
Replace initial correct-skill practice entirely.

cards.answer: Prepare the student to solve problems when events differ from the ideal plan.
cards.explanation: Introduce realistic variables once the skill is being learned and give corrective feedback.

cards.question: Who must personally give the required passenger briefing, and when?

options.text: The tandem PIC, before boarding the aircraft.
The pilot, after takeoff.
The packer, after boarding.
Any DZ employee, at any time before exit.

cards.answer: The tandem PIC, before boarding the aircraft.
cards.explanation: The IRM’s FAR 105.45 implementation states that the PIC cannot delegate this briefing.

cards.question: What subjects belong in the minimum passenger briefing?

options.text: Aircraft/post-exit emergencies, exit, freefall, canopy operation, approach and landing.
Exit and landing only.
Waiver paperwork alone.
Packing, reserve repairs and airworthiness certification.

cards.answer: Aircraft/post-exit emergencies, exit, freefall, canopy operation, approach and landing.
cards.explanation: Practice exit and freefall position and legs-up landing; Category A/B instruction adds ISP skills.
cards.practicePrompt: Deliver the briefing aloud and check the passenger’s understanding.

cards.question: When must the four gear checks occur?

options.text: Before exit, after exit, after deployment, and at landing.
Before boarding only, repeated four times.
Before packing, at takeoff, at opening, and after landing.
Before donning, immediately after donning, before boarding, and before exit.

cards.answer: Before donning, immediately after donning, before boarding, and before exit.
cards.explanation: Each stage has a different purpose. Use manufacturer-specific checks within this framework.
cards.practicePrompt: Walk through all four stages using a training harness.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the check before putting equipment on?

options.text: Check only how snug the leg straps feel.
Confirm that movement in the aircraft caused no changes.
Verify that it is airworthy and appropriate for the student.
Check that goggles are already worn.

cards.answer: Verify that it is airworthy and appropriate for the student.
cards.explanation: Inspect condition, currency and suitability while the equipment is fully accessible.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the check immediately after donning?

options.text: Replace all later checks.
Check only the exit order.
Check only whether the main is packed.
Confirm that it is worn correctly and fits well.

cards.answer: Confirm that it is worn correctly and fits well.
cards.explanation: Verify strap routing, twists, adjustments, stowing and accessible handles.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the pre-boarding check?

options.text: Delay harness fitting until jump run.
Check only the reserve color.
Confirm that the student knows their license number.
Confirm that equipment is configured and ready to jump.

cards.answer: Confirm that equipment is configured and ready to jump.
cards.explanation: Waiting and movement can change fit or cause accessories to be left behind.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the pre-exit check?

options.text: Confirm that everything is still in place and ready after aircraft movement.
Perform the first check of the entire day.
Replace the handles check under drogue.
Check only the student’s enthusiasm.

cards.answer: Confirm that everything is still in place and ready after aircraft movement.
cards.explanation: Use the applicable manufacturer’s hookup and pre-exit procedures.

cards.question: You overlook major misrigging but the rest of the evaluation goes well. What result applies?

options.text: A pass if your score exceeds 75%.
An automatic supervision failure.
Only an air failure if the landing is off target.
Only a warning if the main opens.

cards.answer: An automatic supervision failure.
cards.explanation: Missing major misrigging overrides the numerical supervision score.

cards.question: What connection errors are listed as tandem supervision auto unsats?

options.text: Keeping the student involved in checks.
Performing the final check before setup.
Using a passenger who asks questions.
Missing an attachment or lateral adjustment.

cards.answer: Missing an attachment or lateral adjustment.
cards.explanation: The rubric evaluates correct hookup and fit under manufacturer guidelines.

cards.question: Which environmental checks can produce a supervision auto unsat if missed or violated?

options.text: Only whether the student wants to jump.
Only whether there are clouds somewhere on the horizon.
Only whether the plane reaches maximum altitude.
Acceptable winds, a good spot, and cloud clearance.

cards.answer: Acceptable winds, a good spot, and cloud clearance.
cards.explanation: Failure to confirm acceptable winds and a bad spot/cloud-clearance violation are listed automatic failures.

cards.question: How far does your responsibility for physically supervising the simulated student extend?

options.text: To the aircraft and back to the hangar, including other hazardous training/airport areas.
Only inside the classroom.
Only after hookup.
Only while the evaluator is watching.

cards.answer: To the aircraft and back to the hangar, including other hazardous training/airport areas.
cards.explanation: Direct supervision includes classroom, training aids, landing areas, taxiways and runways.

cards.question: What must you provide just before exit?

options.text: A final skydive briefing and confirmation of student readiness.
Only a reminder to smile at the camera.
A request for the student to improvise the dive flow.
A detailed reserve-packing lecture.

cards.answer: A final skydive briefing and confirmation of student readiness.
cards.explanation: Failure to provide the final briefing before exit is an auto unsat; the rubric also scores readiness.

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: Who leads the Category A tandem exit?

options.text: The student, with no instructor input.
The next group on the aircraft.
The camera flyer.
The instructor; the student observes setup, count and launch.

cards.answer: The instructor; the student observes setup, count and launch.
cards.explanation: This is the instructor-led introduction; the student stays in the prescribed safety position until signaled.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: Who leads the Category B tandem exit?

options.text: The camera flyer always counts.
The instructor must prevent the student from counting.
The student gives the count; the instructor observes and assists as necessary.
The student chooses the spot without supervision.

cards.answer: The student gives the count; the instructor observes and assists as necessary.
cards.explanation: Category B increases student responsibility while the instructor maintains control.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: A Category B student does not start the exit count. What does the IRM describe?

options.text: Wait indefinitely at the door.
Prompt verbally, then with rocking; remain mindful of the spot and exit when necessary.
Ignore the spot to finish the count perfectly.
Require the student to leave independently.

cards.answer: Prompt verbally, then with rocking; remain mindful of the spot and exit when necessary.
cards.explanation: If the count is incorrect, follow their body movement to time the launch and assist when momentum moves outward.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: A student grabs the aircraft door. What is the described correction?

options.text: Continue without addressing the grip.
Ask the camera flyer to pull them off.
Let them keep the door grip during launch.
Return their hands to the safety position and remind them to keep them there.

cards.answer: Return their hands to the safety position and remind them to keep them there.
cards.explanation: Anticipate bracing elbows in seated small-door exits; correct position as necessary.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: When should you signal the student to start the freefall dive flow?

options.text: Only after canopy opening.
Before deploying the drogue.
Before any system checks to save time.
After the handles check and confirmation/correction of neutral body position.

cards.answer: After the handles check and confirmation/correction of neutral body position.
cards.explanation: Category A describes checking position, appropriate correction signals, then a thumbs-up to proceed.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: Who initiates Category B leg extensions and team-turn activities?

options.text: Either person, without communicating which one.
The camera flyer controls the maneuvers.
The student; the instructor supplements only after confirming the student’s initiation.
The instructor performs all inputs while the student watches.

cards.answer: The student; the instructor supplements only after confirming the student’s initiation.
cards.explanation: Let the student lead so they can assess their inputs and effects.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What is the Category B leg-awareness exercise?

options.text: Hold a track for the entire droguefall.
Keep the legs motionless and omit altitude checks.
Extend the legs enough to feel wind on the shins, hold 3 seconds, then return to neutral.
Bend the knees as far as possible for 10 seconds.

cards.answer: Extend the legs enough to feel wind on the shins, hold 3 seconds, then return to neutral.
cards.explanation: The goal is leg awareness rather than generating forward movement.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What does team-turn option 1 involve?

options.text: Continuous 360-degree turns to deployment altitude.
Instructor turns while the student remains entirely passive.
Instructor and student start and stop together, initially using 90-degree turns.
The student releases a connector to steer.

cards.answer: Instructor and student start and stop together, initially using 90-degree turns.
cards.explanation: Teach start-coast-stop and recognizable starting/ending headings; further turns depend on altitude.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What does team-turn option 2 involve?

options.text: The student closes their eyes and waits.
The instructor cancels every student correction.
The instructor starts a slow turn; the student recognizes and stops it.
The instructor starts a fast spin to surprise the student.

cards.answer: The instructor starts a slow turn; the student recognizes and stops it.
cards.explanation: This introduces heading maintenance; observe the counterturn input before returning to neutral.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What does HAALR stand for?

options.text: Heading, Altitude, Arch, Legs, Relax.
Harness, Altimeter, Attachments, Laterals, RSL.
Hands, Aircraft, Altitude, Landing, Reserve.
Heading, Airspeed, Arms, Legs, Ripcord.

cards.answer: Heading, Altitude, Arch, Legs, Relax.
cards.explanation: Use it to scan heading/altitude and maintain a relaxed neutral position.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: A student fails to begin a normal dive-flow task. What is the general progression?

options.text: Prompt with signals, then physically assist if there is no response.
Always complete all movements for them before any signal.
Ignore the omission through deployment.
Immediately abandon altitude awareness to repeat the task.

cards.answer: Prompt with signals, then physically assist if there is no response.
cards.explanation: The IRM has task-specific prompts and assists. Physical techniques must also comply with the manufacturer’s guidance.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What prompts can help a student who is not checking the altimeter?

options.text: Wait until below deployment altitude.
Tell them to check after landing.
Point at the camera only.
Tap the altimeter; if needed move it in front of their face.

cards.answer: Tap the altimeter; if needed move it in front of their face.
cards.explanation: The table uses this for COA/HAALR and the lock-on sequence; continue to protect deployment altitude.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What does the Category A tandem dive-flow chart assign for practice deployment?

options.text: Three practice deployments.
No practice deployments.
One practice deployment under canopy.
Ten practice deployments regardless of altitude.

cards.answer: Three practice deployments.
cards.explanation: The chart shows safe exit, COA, practice deploy three times, then COA and the bottom-end sequence.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What are the Category A/B chart’s tandem lock-on and wave-off/pull altitudes?

options.text: Lock on at 6,000 ft; pull at 5,500 ft, using the solo figures.
Lock on at 3,000 ft; pull at 2,500 ft.
Lock on at 5,000 ft; pull at 4,000 ft.
Lock on at 6,500 ft; wave off and pull at 6,000 ft.

cards.answer: Lock on at 6,500 ft; wave off and pull at 6,000 ft.
cards.explanation: These are the chart’s tandem planned altitudes. Other passages give a 5,000-ft release floor, and UPT course criteria use separate figures. Agree the applicable plan with the examiner; a failure threshold is not a planned pull altitude.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall
Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: The student is behind in the bottom-end sequence. What must you protect?

options.text: A full video sequence before releasing.
Drogue release no lower than 5,000 ft, whether or not the student participates.
Completion of all turns before releasing.
The student’s chance to pull even below 4,000 ft.

cards.answer: Drogue release no lower than 5,000 ft, whether or not the student participates.
cards.explanation: Prompt then immediately assist when needed. The 5,000-ft floor does not replace the higher planned deployment altitude.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall
Category A and B exit and droguefall
Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What duration of instability is a TI air-evaluation auto unsat?

options.text: More than 30 seconds.
Any student arm movement.
More than 10 seconds.
Only instability that lasts until main opening.

cards.answer: More than 10 seconds.
cards.explanation: The list separately includes lack of freefall and droguefall heading control. Do not use a grading threshold as permission to delay correcting instability.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: What does “freefall below 8,000 ft” mean in the TI air-failure list?

options.text: Remaining in the pre-drogue freefall phase below 8,000 ft is an auto unsat.
A main must be fully open by 8,000 ft.
8,000 ft is a normal post-probation opening requirement.
All droguefall must end by 8,000 ft.

cards.answer: Remaining in the pre-drogue freefall phase below 8,000 ft is an auto unsat.
cards.explanation: Keep pre-drogue freefall distinct from droguefall. Follow manufacturer drogue timing and the briefed evaluation plan.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.category: Category A and B exit and droguefall
cards.question: Which checks/control omissions automatically fail the TI air evaluation?

options.text: Omitting HandCam.
Not using outside video.
Not doing a stand-up landing.
Missing droguefall handles checks or inability to control freefall/droguefall heading.

cards.answer: Missing droguefall handles checks or inability to control freefall/droguefall heading.
cards.explanation: Handles checks and heading control are explicit auto-unsat items.

references.section: Category A and B exit and droguefall

cards.question: How does canopy instruction differ between Category A and Category B?

options.text: Both omit pattern instruction.
Category A is instructor-led; Category B is student-led with assistance.
Both require the student to fly independently without assistance.
Category A prohibits student involvement; Category B has no supervision.

cards.answer: Category A is instructor-led; Category B is student-led with assistance.
cards.explanation: Maintain instructor control and safety while progressively increasing the student’s contribution.

cards.question: How should the landing pattern be taught on the ground?

options.text: With an overhead map followed, when possible, by a 3D demonstration in view of the landing area.
By having the student memorize compass directions without landmarks.
Only by pointing vaguely toward the runway.
Only after entering final approach.

cards.answer: With an overhead map followed, when possible, by a 3D demonstration in view of the landing area.
cards.explanation: Use visual orientation and actual landmarks to connect ground planning with canopy flight.
cards.practicePrompt: Teach a pattern using a map and point out the holding area and landmarks.

cards.question: What should the student do with their hands immediately after opening?

options.text: Reach immediately for any available handle.
Grab the instructor’s reserve handle for balance.
Release attachment points independently.
Keep them in the safety position until the instructor hands them the toggles.

cards.answer: Keep them in the safety position until the instructor hands them the toggles.
cards.explanation: This is specified for both Category A and B canopy instruction.

cards.question: How can you teach the student to locate the DZ under canopy?

options.text: Have them stare at the altimeter alone.
Always locate it for them without involving them.
Ask them to locate it only at final approach.
Have them scan from the horizon to straight down, turning and repeating as needed.

cards.answer: Have them scan from the horizon to straight down, turning and repeating as needed.
cards.explanation: Category A introduces the process; Category B checks that they can repeat it independently.

cards.question: Why should the student read canopy altitude aloud?

options.text: To entertain the camera flyer.
To replace the instructor’s own altitude awareness.
So they never need to look outside.
So the instructor can confirm reading accuracy and check frequency.

cards.answer: So the instructor can confirm reading accuracy and check frequency.
cards.explanation: Combine altitude with position, landmarks, traffic and pattern awareness.

cards.question: When should you practice flaring for landing?

options.text: Well before entering the landing pattern.
Only after touchdown.
Only if the student asks at the last second.
Only on final approach at low altitude.

cards.answer: Well before entering the landing pattern.
cards.explanation: Prepare the student early while maintaining traffic awareness and adequate altitude.

cards.question: What wind effects should canopy instruction demonstrate?

options.text: Only the direction of the windsock.
Running, holding, crosswind drift and crabbing to correct it.
Only how to perform steep turns near the ground.
Only the canopy’s color and size.

cards.answer: Running, holding, crosswind drift and crabbing to correct it.
cards.explanation: Connect wind direction/speed to ground speed and ground track.

cards.question: What teaching approach is described when the student is confused about the canopy flight plan?

options.text: Let confusion continue until landing.
Give vague encouragement without direction.
Remove all participation immediately in every case.
Use prompt, specific commands with familiar radio-style terminology; take toggles as a last resort.

cards.answer: Use prompt, specific commands with familiar radio-style terminology; take toggles as a last resort.
cards.explanation: For example, direct a specific turn back to the holding area. Safety remains the instructor’s responsibility.

cards.question: Which additional canopy demonstrations are identified for Category B?

options.text: An intentional cutaway.
Canopy formation docking.
Braked turns from Category F and the low-turn-recovery drill from Category H.
Intentional low hook turns in the pattern.

cards.answer: Braked turns from Category F and the low-turn-recovery drill from Category H.
cards.explanation: These are instructional demonstrations in appropriate conditions and altitude, not permission to perform hazardous low turns.

cards.question: What should you explain about the tandem legs-up landing position?

options.text: It eliminates the need for flare training.
It is inappropriate for solo-student landings.
It is required on every solo jump.
It replaces all solo landing training.

cards.answer: It is inappropriate for solo-student landings.
cards.explanation: Explicitly distinguish tandem and solo landing body positions.

cards.question: A student cannot follow toggle directions reliably. What option does the IRM describe for landing?

options.text: Have them operate the reserve handle instead.
Allow them to keep controlling the flare without correction.
Skip the landing briefing.
Remove their hands from the toggles and have them mimic inputs, unless using hands to lift legs.

cards.answer: Remove their hands from the toggles and have them mimic inputs, unless using hands to lift legs.
cards.explanation: Adjust participation to preserve a safe landing.

cards.question: What is the “Good” landing-accuracy rubric descriptor?

options.text: A stand-up landing regardless of safety or distance.
Within 60 ft is the minimum for every passing evaluation.
A safe, effective landing within 82 ft of the target, with appropriate landing-type judgment.
Any landing inside 300 ft automatically earns Good.

cards.answer: A safe, effective landing within 82 ft of the target, with appropriate landing-type judgment.
cards.explanation: The “Excellent” descriptor uses 60 ft. These are rubric descriptors; the overall score and auto-unsat rules still apply.

cards.question: How should the debrief begin?

options.text: By completing paperwork without discussion.
Promptly, in a suitable environment, with a student-led review of positive aspects.
Only after the next load departs.
With a long instructor monologue listing every error.

cards.answer: Promptly, in a suitable environment, with a student-led review of positive aspects.
cards.explanation: Use questions to reinforce what went well and help the student assess their performance.
cards.practicePrompt: Ask a simulated student what went well before supplying your observations.

cards.question: How many grouped improvement points does the tandem debrief rubric call for?

options.text: Exactly one, regardless of the performance.
None if the student enjoyed the jump.
As many as you can think of, without priorities.
Three to five, prioritized by safety and goals, with fixes and retraining.

cards.answer: Three to five, prioritized by safety and goals, with fixes and retraining.
cards.explanation: The Good descriptor includes retraining at least one safety/goal-related improvement; Excellent covers all safety/goal-related points.

cards.question: The instructor identifies an error but gives no corrective retraining. What can result?

options.text: An automatic supervision failure.
A guaranteed pass if the student agrees.
Only a lower video score.
No consequence after landing.

cards.answer: An automatic supervision failure.
cards.explanation: Corrective retraining and limiting improvement points with fixes are explicit supervision auto-unsat requirements.

cards.question: What records and next steps should close the debrief?

options.text: Leave all goals and progression decisions to the student without guidance.
Only ask for a review of the DZ.
Only record the instructor’s jump count.
Review freefall/canopy goals, complete the logbook and progression card, and establish next steps.

cards.answer: Review freefall/canopy goals, complete the logbook and progression card, and establish next steps.
cards.explanation: The rubric rewards student self-assessment and correctly completed records.
cards.practicePrompt: Have the student explain goals, assess them, and complete the logbook for you to check.
